summary: Introductory discovery between Redwood AE/SE and EmberCore platform leads to scope pilot for GPU onramp. Main themes: existing infra and constraints (on-prem vs VPC), required SLAs and security posture (SOC 2, KMS, audit logs), and a proof-of-concept plan to run benchmarks against EmberCore workloads. Action items assigned for pricing, benchmark runbook, and compliance owners.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: Tue, 2026-06-30
Start time: 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Amina Chowdhury (EmberCore CTO), Benji Li (EmberCore Head of Platform), Marco Reyes (EmberCore SRE)
Links shared: EmberCore infra diagram (ask Samira for link), Redwood quickstart deck (sent in chat), benchmark template spreadsheet (referenced)

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, I'm Samira from Redwood, AE on this account. Diego my SE is here. hows it going at EmberCore?
[00:12] Amina: Hey Samira, good to meet you both. We, uh, excited to chat — we got, hm, some pressure to get inference off our cluster into something more predictable.
[00:23] Diego: Nice to meet you Amina. Quick agenda — understand current infra, constraints (on-prem vs cloud), security bar, and define pilot scope. Sound right?
[00:30] Benji: Yep, that works. We also want to understand where Redwood sits vs doing our own stack or pushing everything to CloudGiant.
[00:40] Samira: Totally. We'll talk tradeoffs — latency, cost, control. Quick qualifier: what does your GPU footprint look like today?
[00:49] Amina: Uh, so we run mostly on prem in two colo sites. We have, um, about 24 A100-ish nodes, mixed gens, some 80GB, some 40s. Planned 12 more by Q4.
[00:59] Marco: To add, we use our own provisioning layer — it's kinda homegrown, runs on top of kuburnetis, we call it ember-orch.
[01:09] Diego: Got it, kuburnetis, ember-orch. How much traffic is inference vs training?
[01:14] Benji: Inference is about 70% of the load, training is weekly. Latencies are sensitive: 99th is sub-200ms for some endpoints.
[01:25] Samira: Understood. Sounds like predictable throughput and latency are important. Do you have any compliance constraints — SOC 2, data residency?
[01:33] Amina: SOC 2 in-flight, we need audit logs, SSO with Okta, and want to integrate with our Hashi KMS — or HSM eventually.
[01:42] Samira: That's a common ask. Redwood Private offers VPC/private control plane and KMS/HSM integrations. For hosted we can do customer-managed keys too — we'll share the whitepaper.
[01:52] Benji: Clarify hosted vs dedicated — hosted means we send traffic to Redwood's cloud endpoint, dedicated means reserved GPU capacity in region?
[02:00] Diego: Yes. Hosted is fastest to launch, but dedicated gives you isolated capacity, predictable throughput and more control over model variants and caching. There's also a private deployment option for VPC/on-prem.
[02:13] Amina: If we do hosted, passing PCI-esque data isn't ideal. We probably need VPC or on-prem for some endpoints.
[02:20] Samira: Makes sense. We can do a hybrid — some low-risk traffic to hosted, sensitive stuff routed to your dedicated/private deployment. Redwood's smart routing can help.
[02:33] Marco: Can you speak to latency overhead for hosted calls? We run sub-200ms now on local infra. A 50ms penalty is acceptable; larger is not.
[02:42] Diego: Typical added latency depends on region and model size. For medium-sized open models we often see 20–60ms more for hosted regional endpoints. For 8B-13B models quantized on GPU we can get similar p99 if you use dedicated with colocated region. But there's variability — we'd love to run a local benchmark.
[02:59] Benji: Cost — roughly ballpark if we had 30M tokens a month, how does hosted compare to dedicated commit?
[03:08] Samira: We'll send a pricing matrix, but rough: hosted per-token is higher at low commit; dedicated reserve reduces unit cost. Optimize via batching and prefix caching too — Redwood Optimize can suggest profiles.
[03:22] Amina: What about private on-prem deploy? Do you ship runnable packages?
[03:27] Diego: Yes, we have a private deployment that runs with a customer-managed control plane and optional air-gapped package. It integrates with your k8s layer or can run on bare metal. Some telemetry is optional/masked for compliance.
[03:41] Marco: That sounds promising. Our biggest blocker historically is KV cache management across pods — cache misses kill p99. How does Redwood handle KV cache and batching?
[03:50] Diego: The runtime does continuous batching and smart KV cache affinity. We have options for shared KV cache on dedicated pools and policies for affinity to keep hot sessions on the same executor. There's tricky edge cases but we can show the architecture.
[04:06] Benji: Are there any required agent installs for the on-prem runtime?
[04:10] Samira: We ship a lightweight runtime with a containerized agent. It's not an agent that phones home with payloads — it's just for orchestration and health.
[04:19] Amina: Security specifics — what about audit logs, retention, and role-based access?
[04:24] Diego: We support token-level audit logs, RBAC via SAML/Okta, and retention policies. For private deployments logs can be stored in your ELK/CloudWatch equivalent. We'll share diagrams.
[04:37] Benji: Who at Redwood handles the compliance integration — is that the SE or a security team?
[04:42] Samira: Diego as SE will own the technical runbook, and we have a dedicated security/compliance team for deeper audits; I'll introduce them after we get to the compliance checklist phase.
[04:52] Marco: On the model side — are you supporting custom models? We're looking at deploying a forked Llama variant with custom tokenization.
[04:59] Diego: We onboard custom models. There are steps — model packaging, performance profile runs, and quantization recommendations. For tokenization differences we validate the tokenizer and KV cache behavior.
[05:12] Amina: Timeline — we want a pilot before Q3, ideally in July. Is that feasible?
[05:18] Samira: Yes. Pilot could be a small set of endpoints routed to dedicated pool or private deploy. We'll propose a 4-week pilot: week 0 setup, week 1 baseline runs, week 2 optimizations, week 3 readouts.
[05:30] Benji: That sounds reasonable. What do you need from us to scope the pilot?
[05:35] Diego: Test corpus, traffic shape (RPS + payload sizes), target p99/p50, model versions, and a list of endpoints you want in-scope. Also, access to a staging environment if we do private deploy.
[05:48] Amina: We'll produce the corpus and a short backlog of endpoints.
[05:52] Samira: Great. Competitors — you mentioned CloudGiant earlier. Any other options you're evaluating?
[05:57] Benji: FastServe.ai and also some internal plans to build a mini-served cluster.
[06:03] Samira: Good to know. We'll highlight tradeoffs in the follow-up doc.
[06:08] [10 minute mark - brief pause while people glance at shared deck]
[06:12] Diego: Quick note on fallbacks — Redwood supports automated fallback policies: if dedicated pool is saturated we can route to hosted compatible model to keep availability.
[06:22] Marco: That must be validated for context/kv consistency though — otherwise responses can diverge.
[06:27] Diego: Yes, model variants need to be compatible. We can pin model versions and have deterministic fallback mapping.
[06:36] Benji: For observability what do you surface? Token-level cost, per-route dashboards, errors?
[06:41] Samira: All of that — token breakdown, latency heatmaps, tracing hooks, and per-model regression alerts tied to evaluation prompt sets.
[06:52] Amina: Can we route selectively by tag or header so only non-sensitive calls go to hosted?
[06:58] Diego: Yes, routing policies can be header-based or route-based. You control the policy.
[07:04] Benji: Data residency — some customers are strict about eu-only processing. Can you guarantee region pinning?
[07:10] Samira: Yes, for Dedicated and Private we can ensure region pinning. Hosted can be region-scoped but dedicated is better for strict residency.
[07:19] Marco: Benchmarks — what will you need to run an apples-to-apples run?
[07:24] Diego: We need the model binary (or an image), sample request corpus, payload sizes, target RPS, and a staging endpoint or access to the infra for private deploy. Also version pins for tokenizer and any custom pre/post processing.
[07:38] Amina: We'll prepare that. Question: how do you handle model rollout / A/B testing? We want to do controlled rollouts.
[07:45] Samira: We support canary deploys, A/B tests, and automatic fallback. You can set traffic percentages per variant and Redwood Console shows comparative metrics.
[07:57] Benji: Pricing ask again — what about network egress for hosted? Big factor for us.
[08:03] Samira: Egress is usually billed by region (if we host in region X). For private/on-prem that's not applicable. We'll include egress examples in the pricing sheet.
[08:12] [Short back and forth clarifying questions about network topology and peering]
[08:30] Marco: One more technical — how do you support multi-GPU models and model parallelism? Our largest models use tensor parallel.
[08:38] Diego: We support multi-GPU serving for large models via model parallelism and optimized kernels. We pick kernel variants based on architecture and sequence length. For private deploy we can tune node GPU affinities.
[08:52] Amina: Any red flags you usually see with on-prem customers?
[08:57] Samira: Common ones: network constraints (latency/peering), logging/telemetry restrictions, and differences in GPU gens causing perf variance. We mitigate by pre-onboarding perf profiles and a short calibration run.
[09:10] Benji: Great. Let's talk pilot success metrics — what are realistic goals?
[09:14] Diego: I'd propose: match baseline p99 within X% (configurable), 20–30% reduction in token unit cost vs your current unoptimized run, and stable error rate < 0.5% for latency spikes.
[09:28] Amina: We can agree on p99 baseline target. We'll also want a security checklist completed.
[09:34] Samira: Perfect. Action items and next steps: we'll send a follow-up with pricing, SOC2 doc, and a pilot runbook. Can we tentatively schedule the technical deep dive with Marco the week of July 6?
[09:45] Marco: That works for me after 10am PT any day.
[09:48] Samira: I'll propose slots in the calendar.
[09:51] Benji: Any blockers from legal or procurement we should flag now?
[09:55] Amina: Procurement will want standard MSA and SLAs. Not a blocker but process takes 3–4 weeks.
[10:02] Samira: Understood — we'll surface standard MSA terms and sample SLA in the follow-up.
[10:08] [Crosstalk, laughter]
[10:12] Diego: Quick note — Diego to lead the benchmark runbook and will need the test corpus. Samira will send pricing and compliance docs.
[10:20] Amina: Sounds good. Thanks, this was useful.
[10:24] Samira: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with materials and proposed slots.
[10:28] Benji: Thanks.
[10:30] Marco: Bye.

End recap (verbatim to notes):
- Pilot: 4-week pilot to run in July — scope: 3 endpoints, run baseline + optimize + readout.
- Data required from EmberCore: test corpus, traffic shape, staging access for private deploy if chosen.
- Docs to send: hosted vs dedicated pricing, SOC2 & KMS integration notes, sample SLA and MSA.
- Owners: Samira (pricing/docs), Diego (benchmarks/runbook), Amina (confirm compliance stakeholders).

Transcript notes: occasional mis-transcriptions present ("kuburnetis" for Kubernetes, "Redwood Dediated" in one automated line), some speaker labels generic in chunks.
